html:
The Hualapai are a Yuman-speaking people of northwestern Arizona, on the plateaus along the south side of the Grand Canyon. Their name means people of the tall pines. They are close kin to the Havasupai, whose language they share.

They lived in bands that farmed small plots near springs, gathered agave, pine nuts and seeds, and hunted deer and bighorn sheep. They traded with the Mojave and with peoples to the east.

When miners and freight roads came into their land in the 1860s, the Hualapai fought the United States army from 1865 to about 1870. In 1874 the army marched them south to a camp on the Colorado River, where many died. They walked home, and in 1883 a reservation was set aside along the canyon. Today about 2,300 enrolled Hualapai run tourism there, including the glass Skywalk over the canyon. See also Walapai.
